deep.reconstruction:
There is no mathematics on this page. It is a fair copy of lecture notes on ancient history, covering the end of the Achaemenid Persian Empire. It continues the previous page on Artaxerxes II and leads into the next page, 'Dritter Abschnitt der Geschichte. Griechische Staaten'. The arrangement and periodisation resemble a Göttingen-style universal-history course, such as Heeren's lectures or his Handbuch der Geschichte der Staaten des Alterthums; that attribution is my conjecture. The narrative runs as follows:

(1) Artaxerxes II had, besides his legitimate sons, 115 illegitimate ones. Among the legitimate sons, Darius was the designated successor. He conspired with 50 others, but the plot was discovered.

(2) Egypt and the Phoenicians rose against Persia. Artaxerxes II died in 362; modern dating is 359/358 BC.

(3) His youngest son Ochus succeeded him as Artaxerxes III. He was a cruel ruler who secured the throne by exterminating the royal family.

(4) He reconquered Egypt. The date reads like '384', but historically this was 343/342 BC. The empire briefly revived, but this did not last.

(5) Mentor and Bagoas divided power between them. In 338 Bagoas killed the king and enthroned the youngest son Arses, whom he murdered in 336.

(6) Darius III Codomannus then took the throne and had Bagoas executed. He was a contemporary of Alexander the Great, who attacked the already weakened empire. In 330 Darius died 'in Alexander's hands'.

There is no derivation to reconstruct. Within this bundle the page is out of place relative to its 'Lagrange' label. The hand and content suggest notes from a history lecture, perhaps Gauss's student-era notes or someone else's, rather than mathematical work.
errors: Historical: Artaxerxes II's death is given as 362; modern dating is 359/358 BC. Older chronologies varied, so this is not necessarily a slip of the writer.

Historical or reading problem: the reconquest of Egypt by Artaxerxes III is dated '384' on the page. The actual date is c. 343/342 BC; 384 precedes his reign and is impossible. Most likely the writer intended 344 or 343, or the digit is misread.
Historical: Darius III did not die at Alexander's hands. He was murdered by Bessus and fellow satraps in 330 BC while fleeing Alexander. The notes compress this.
Minor: '115 unächte' illegitimate sons follows Justin's figure (115); this is consistent with the source tradition, not an error.

results.what: Lecture notes on late Achaemenid history (Artaxerxes II to Darius III); no mathematical content
results.usually_credited_to: standard 18th-century universal-history textbooks (e.g., Heeren, Gatterer, Schlözer tradition), ancient sources Justin/Plutarch/Diodorus

deep.surprise_reason: The page contains no mathematics, only routine history lecture notes. That such notes exist among Gauss's papers (possibly from his Göttingen student years) is of minor biographical interest only.

checkable.asserts: Reign length of Artaxerxes III implied by the page's dates (accession 362, death 338): 24 years
Reign of Arses per the page: 338 to 336 BC, 2 years
Reign of Darius III per the page: 336 to 330 BC, 6 years

transcription_corrections: Line 2: 'nachfolger aus dem Vater' is probably 'Nachfolger von dem Vater' or similar; the word is uncertain.

Line 4: 'Die Persen verbreiteten sich auch gegen' is doubtful. Context (revolt of Egypt and Phoenicia) suggests something like 'Die ... empörten sich auch gegen' or 'Die Perser verbreiteten sich'; it needs re-examination of the image.
Line 10: '384, bekam er Aegypten wieder': the date is historically impossible; it should be checked as a possible '344'/'343' or a writer's slip.
Line 11: 'eine kurze[?] Zeit aber das schwere[?] des Reichs' may read 'eine kräftige Zeit, aber der Schimmer des Reichs dauerte nicht viel' (uncertain).
Line 16: 'bracht[?] er Bagoas hin richten[?]' should read 'ließ er Bagoas hinrichten'.
Line 1: the struck-through word before 'den ächten' is 'Darius', correctly marked as deleted.
